title: Academic Reading — Practice test 2

parts.title: Passage 1
parts.heading: The Return of the Tram
paragraphs: In the first half of the twentieth century, trams were a familiar sight in hundreds of cities around the world. By the 1960s, however, most of them had disappeared. Cars had become affordable for ordinary families, and city planners regarded trams as slow, noisy relics that blocked the roads. In Britain alone, more than 200 tram networks were closed, and the rails were either removed or simply covered with asphalt.

Today, the tram is making a remarkable comeback. Since the 1980s, more than 150 new systems have opened in Europe, and cities as different as Dubai, Casablanca and Sydney have followed. The modern vehicles bear little resemblance to their predecessors. They are quiet, run on electricity and have low floors, which means that passengers with pushchairs or wheelchairs can board without climbing steps.

Part of the attraction for city authorities is cost. A tram line is considerably cheaper to build than an underground railway, typically costing between a quarter and a third as much per kilometre, because there is no need to dig tunnels. At the same time, a tram can carry far more passengers than a bus. A single modern tram may hold up to 300 people, roughly three times the capacity of a large bus, and it requires only one driver.

Trams also have an effect on how people perceive public transport. Researchers have noticed that the opening of a tram line often attracts car drivers who would never consider taking a bus. Because the rails are permanent and visible, residents and businesses feel confident that the service will continue, and property values near tram stops frequently rise. In the French city of Strasbourg, for example, shops along the new tram route reported an increase in customers within two years of its opening.

Nevertheless, building a tram network is rarely straightforward. Construction can take several years and causes considerable disruption to traffic and local businesses. Underground pipes and cables often have to be moved before the rails can be laid, and this work is frequently more complicated than expected. In Edinburgh, the first line opened in 2014, three years late and well over its original budget, and it was much shorter than originally planned.

Critics also point out that trams are inflexible. A bus route can be changed overnight if a new housing estate is built, whereas a tram line is fixed for decades. Some transport experts therefore argue that modern electric buses running in their own dedicated lanes can offer many of the same benefits at a fraction of the cost. Supporters of trams reply that such bus lanes are often given back to cars when political priorities change, something that is far less likely to happen to rails.

parts.title: Passage 2
parts.heading: Do Plants Communicate?
paragraphs: A

The idea that plants might communicate with one another was, until recently, dismissed by most botanists as fanciful. Plants have no brain and no nervous system, and they cannot move from place to place. Yet over the past four decades, a series of carefully designed experiments has shown that plants are far from passive. They sense their surroundings, respond to threats and, it now appears, exchange information with their neighbours.
B

The first clues came from studies of trees under attack by insects. In the early 1980s, researchers noticed that willow trees growing near trees infested with caterpillars produced chemicals that made their leaves harder to digest, even though they themselves had not been attacked. Their findings were widely criticised at the time, partly because the experiments were difficult to repeat, but similar results have since been obtained with many different species.
C

The most widely accepted channel of communication is the air. When a plant is damaged, it releases a mixture of volatile chemicals into the atmosphere. Neighbouring plants that detect these chemicals begin to strengthen their own defences before any insect arrives. In one field experiment, tobacco plants growing next to clipped sagebrush suffered significantly less damage from insects over the following season than plants growing next to undamaged sagebrush.
D

Some of these airborne signals also work on other creatures. Certain plants, when eaten by caterpillars, release chemicals that attract wasps which lay their eggs inside the caterpillars, eventually killing them. In effect, the plant is calling for help. Farmers in East Africa have used this knowledge in a system known as push-pull, in which plants that repel pests are grown among crops, while plants that attract them are grown around the edge of the field.
E

A more controversial suggestion is that plants communicate below ground. The roots of most plants are connected to networks of fungi, which supply them with water and minerals in exchange for sugars. Some scientists claim that these networks also carry warning signals and even nutrients from one plant to another, so that older trees can support young seedlings growing in their shade. Others argue that the evidence is weaker than popular accounts suggest, and that many studies have been too small to draw firm conclusions.
F

Whatever the mechanism, researchers are careful about the words they use. To say that plants talk or have feelings, they warn, is misleading. A plant does not intend to warn its neighbours; it simply releases chemicals, and other plants have evolved to take advantage of them. Most botanists therefore prefer to speak of signalling rather than communication in the human sense.
G

The practical applications could nevertheless be significant. If crops could be encouraged to raise their defences before pests arrive, farmers might be able to use far fewer pesticides. Several research groups are now testing sprays that imitate the chemicals released by damaged plants, although so far the results in large fields have been less impressive than those obtained in laboratories.

parts.title: Passage 3
parts.heading: Why We Put Things Off
paragraphs: A

Almost everyone procrastinates at least occasionally, but for a significant minority the habit is chronic. Surveys suggest that around 20 per cent of adults regularly delay important tasks to the point where it harms their work, finances or health, and the figure among university students is considerably higher. Procrastination, in other words, is not a minor quirk but a problem with real consequences.
B

For a long time it was assumed that procrastinators were simply lazy or bad at managing their time. Psychologists now believe this explanation is largely mistaken. Many chronic procrastinators work extremely hard on tasks they enjoy, and teaching them to use diaries and to-do lists makes surprisingly little difference. The problem, it seems, lies not in how people organise their time but in how they manage their emotions.
C

According to this view, we put off tasks that make us feel bad, whether because they are boring, difficult or associated with the fear of failure. Delaying the task brings immediate relief, and this relief makes it more likely that we will delay again next time. The pattern resembles other short-term coping strategies: it feels good now but creates greater stress later, when the deadline approaches.
D

Interestingly, perfectionism appears to play a part. People who set impossibly high standards for themselves may avoid starting a task because any result is likely to fall short. I find this one of the more convincing findings in the field, because it explains why some of the most capable students are also the worst procrastinators. For them, an unfinished essay can never be judged a failure.
E

Another factor is the way we think about our future selves. Brain-imaging studies have found that when people think about themselves in ten years' time, the pattern of activity resembles the one produced when they think about a stranger. If the future self feels like someone else, it becomes easier to leave the hard work to that person. Exercises that help people imagine their future selves in vivid detail have been shown to increase saving for retirement, and some researchers believe they might reduce procrastination too.
F

What, then, can be done? Simply telling procrastinators to try harder is unlikely to work. More promising approaches involve reducing the unpleasant feelings attached to a task, for example by breaking it into very small steps or by agreeing to work on it for just five minutes. Once started, people often find the task less unpleasant than they expected and continue. Being kind to oneself also seems to help: in one study, students who forgave themselves for procrastinating before a first exam procrastinated less before the next one.
G

None of this means that every delay is harmful. Some writers claim that a short period of delay allows ideas to develop, and there may be some truth in this. However, it would be wrong to treat chronic procrastination as a creative strategy. For most people who struggle with it, the cost in stress and missed opportunities is far greater than any benefit, and the sooner they understand its emotional roots, the better.

questions.text: Procrastination is a minor problem for most people who suffer from it chronically.
questions.evidence: Procrastination, in other words, is not a minor quirk but a problem with real consequences.

questions.explain_vi: Sinh viên tha thứ cho bản thân thì lần sau ít trì hoãn hơn, và tác giả trình bày điều này như cách 'seems to help' → YES.

questions.text: According to paragraph C, why do people delay unpleasant tasks?

because delaying makes them feel better at once

doing it together with a friend
rewarding yourself when it is finished
doing it first thing in the morning
